canonical_statement: The review aimed to quantify pooled diagnostic accuracy of LLM-based rare-disease systems, identify sources of heterogeneity, and assess methodological quality and clinical readiness.
The systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA-DTA guidance and was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework before data extraction.
Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, arXiv, and medRxiv) were searched from January 2020 through February 2026 with no language restriction.
Eligible studies used at least one LLM as the primary diagnostic reasoning component, evaluated rare-disease diagnosis in more than 10 cases, and reported strict Recall@1.

population.label: Studies of LLM-based rare-disease diagnosis
inclusion_criteria: LLM is primary diagnostic reasoning component
exclusion_criteria: only Recall@k with k>1 or mention-in-differential without extractable R@1
gene prioritisation rather than disease diagnosis
LLM only a component in a non-LLM ranking algorithm

canonical_statement: Screening, full-text assessment, data extraction, and quality assessment were independently performed by at least two authors, with disagreements resolved by consensus.
Inter-rater agreement was 92.0% (Cohen kappa 0.64) for title/abstract screening and 76.9% (kappa 0.54) for full-text assessment.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Cohen kappa 0.64 for title/abstract screening; 0.54 for full-text assessment.

canonical_statement: The review extracted study, system, benchmark, sample-size, input-modality, and strict R@1 data and used pre-specified entry-selection rules to reduce within-paper correlation.

Risk of bias was assessed with a modified QUADAS-3 instrument covering participant selection, index test conduct, target condition, flow/timing, data leakage, reproducibility, and evaluation fairness; any high domain made the overall rating high.

The primary meta-analysis used Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformed proportions and a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model; 95% prediction intervals, I-squared and tau-squared heterogeneity, subgroup Q tests, Egger testing, and multiple sensitivity analyses were also used.
The search identified 902 records; after 338 duplicates were removed, 564 records were screened, 78 full texts were assessed, and 15 studies contributing 19 system-dataset entries were included.

population.label: Records and studies in the review

canonical_statement: The meta-analysis comprised 15 studies and 19 system-dataset entries published from 2024 to 2026; 17 of 19 entries were from 2025 or later and the abstract reports 39,529 total cases.

population.label: Included LLM rare-disease diagnostic evaluations; 19 system-dataset entries; total N=39,529 cases

canonical_statement: Across 19 system-dataset entries, pooled Recall@1 was 43.3% (95% CI 35.1-51.6), with I-squared 99.6% and a 95% prediction interval of 11.6-78.3%.

population.label: 19 system-dataset entries from 15 studies; total N=39,529 cases

canonical_statement: REML sensitivity analysis produced pooled Recall@1 of 43.2% (95% CI 35.2-51.5) with a 95% prediction interval of 11.9-78.0%.
REML with Hartung-Knapp adjustment produced pooled Recall@1 of 43.2% (95% CI 34.6-52.1) with a 95% prediction interval of 10.2-80.2%.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses produced pooled Recall@1 estimates ranging from 41.1% to 44.7%.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Source reports range 41.1-44.7%; midpoint used only as structured estimate field.

canonical_statement: Restricting to studies with a peer-reviewed citation at extraction yielded pooled Recall@1 of 38.0% (95% CI 26.8-49.9; k=8; I-squared 99.7%) with a 95% prediction interval of 9.2-72.5%.
Excluding two studies with N <=100 yielded pooled Recall@1 of 40.0% (95% CI 31.5-48.9) with a 95% prediction interval of 9.7-75.5%.

population.label: Meta-analysis excluding two studies with N <=100

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Pooled Recall@1 after excluding small studies (%)

canonical_statement: Excluding two Phenopacket Store entries with overlapping case pools increased pooled Recall@1 to 46.0% (95% CI 37.7-54.5).

population.label: Meta-analysis excluding two overlapping Phenopacket Store entries

canonical_statement: Egger regression did not indicate publication bias (z=0.72, p=0.480).

In the meta-analysis pool, RareBench entries had pooled Recall@1 of 52.0% (95% CI 40.7-63.2; k=6) versus 21.7% (95% CI 18.2-25.5; k=2) on Phenopacket Store; the between-benchmark difference was significant (Qbetween=26.53, p<0.001).
Ultra-rare diseases comprised 52.8% of Phenopacket Store, 29.3% of aggregate RareBench, 30.1% of MAC Medline, and 1.7% of the Chinese Rare Disease List.

In the post-hoc prevalence-accuracy analysis, standalone LLM accuracy showed a negative trend with benchmark ultra-rare disease proportion (R-squared=0.55; -5.8 percentage points in R@1 per 10% increase in ultra-rare proportion).

population.label: Benchmarks represented in post-hoc prevalence-accuracy analysis

quantitative_result.effect_measure: R@1 percentage-point change per 10% increase in ultra-rare proportion

canonical_statement: Augmented systems (agent-based, retrieval-augmented, or domain-specific fine-tuned; k=8) achieved pooled Recall@1 of 52.5% (95% CI 42.0-62.9) versus 35.4% (95% CI 30.6-40.4) for standalone LLMs (k=11; p=0.004).

population.label: 19 system-dataset entries partitioned by augmentation strategy

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Standalone 95% CI 30.6-40.4; augmented I2=99.4%; standalone I2=98.1%.

canonical_statement: Across four matched within-paper comparisons on the same benchmark, every augmented system outperformed its baseline, with absolute R@1 improvements ranging from 4.5 to 36 percentage points.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Reported absolute R@1 improvement range midpoint (percentage points)
quantitative_result.original_result_text: Source reports range 4.5 to 36 percentage points; midpoint is used only to satisfy the structured estimate field.

canonical_statement: For MINT, R@1 was 47.6% on diseases present in its training set versus 7.0% on diseases absent from training; on unseen diseases, a retrieval-augmented baseline achieved 13.8%.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: R@1 on diseases present in training set (%)

canonical_statement: RareSeek achieved R@1 of 68.4% on institutional data used for fine-tuning and 39.2% on the independent RareBench benchmark.
Input modality was not a significant moderator: pooled R@1 was 39.6% for structured HPO input versus 47.3% for unstructured clinical text (p=0.35).

population.label: Meta-analysis entries grouped by input modality

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Pooled R@1 with structured HPO input (%)

canonical_statement: In DeepRare, adding exome sequencing data to phenotypic input was associated with R@1 of 69.1% versus 57.2% with HPO-only input.
In RareSeek, variant-only input using pre-identified pathogenic variants in GA4GH Phenopackets yielded R@1 of 47.9%.
All 19 system-dataset entries were rated high overall risk of bias; potential data leakage was rated high risk in 18 of 19 entries.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Entries rated high overall risk of bias

canonical_statement: No included study provided independent external-group replication, prospective clinical validation, or evaluation of real-world outcomes such as time to diagnosis.
The authors identified that 1,122 of 2,185 RareBench public-component cases (51%) came from public benchmark sources released before the approximate April 2023 cutoff of GPT-4 1106-preview.

concept.text: Cases from pre-cutoff public benchmark sources

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Proportion of cases from pre-cutoff public benchmark sources (%)

canonical_statement: DeepRare ablation on LIRICAL showed that removing similar-case retrieval reduced GPT-4o R@1 from 51.6% to 39.5%, a 12-percentage-point loss attributed by the authors to retrieval over a benchmark-overlapping corpus.

For benchmark prevalence mapping, the authors mapped diseases to Orphanet prevalence categories; mapping rates were 49.1% for Phenopacket Store and 88-91% for RareBench, MAC Medline, and the Chinese Rare Disease List.

Inspection of 9,588 Phenopacket Store JSON files found at least one pre-identified causal variant in every case; among 10,547 variant entries, 94.4% had full VCF-format records and 99.9% carried a pathogenic or likely pathogenic ACMG classification.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: Variant entries with full VCF-format records (%)

canonical_statement: The primary DerSimonian-Laird model did not account for within-paper correlation, although pre-defined entry-selection rules were used to mitigate it.

Substantial heterogeneity across benchmarks, input modalities, evaluation protocols, and disease composition limited comparability and made pooled estimates descriptive rather than predictive of clinical performance.
Some included evaluations used constrained candidate lists rather than open-ended diagnostic generation, complicating cross-study interpretation of R@1.
The benchmark prevalence analysis covered only a subset of benchmarks and had variable Orphanet mapping rates of about 49-91%, making ultra-rare prevalence estimates approximate.
Focusing on R@1 did not capture the full clinical utility of diagnostic-support systems, including differential-list performance, gene/variant interpretation, and phenotype refinement.
Four meta-analysis entries relied on approximate R@1 values extracted from figures.

The review excluded gene-prioritisation studies and hybrid LLM-traditional systems from quantitative synthesis, so its pooled findings apply to rare-disease diagnosis rather than those complementary tasks.

The authors concluded that current retrospective benchmark evidence does not establish clinical utility and that prospective studies should assess diagnostic accuracy, downstream testing, time to diagnosis, and clinical decision-making.
The authors considered inference-time access to external knowledge promising for rare-disease diagnosis but explicitly conditioned that potential on validation in real-world settings.

The work was supported by NIH Common Fund, NHGRI grant 15-HG-0130, NINDS U01NS134349, NLM R00LM014429, and the Potocsnak Center for Undiagnosed and Rare Disorders; the funders were reported to have no role in design, analysis, publication decision, or manuscript preparation.
The authors stated that meta-analysis data and benchmark prevalence-mapping files will be made available in a public GitHub repository upon publication.
The authors stated that computation scripts, forest-plot code, and the manuscript build pipeline will be made available in the same public GitHub repository upon publication.
